opus-5.5.text:
I think the most important thing we got right was openness. From the very beginning, when Mark Zuckerberg asked me to create FAIR back in 2013, I set a few conditions. One was that we would do open research: publish our papers, release our code, and engage with the academic community as real participants, not just consumers of their work. A lot of people at the time thought that was naive for a corporate lab. Why give away your advantage?

But the reality is that nobody has a monopoly on good ideas. Progress in AI comes from the whole community, and if you close yourself off, you fall behind. When you publish, you attract the best scientists, because good researchers want their work to be seen and recognized. And you get feedback much faster, because other people pick up your work, test it, find the flaws, and improve on it.

The best illustration is PyTorch. It came out of FAIR, we open-sourced it, and it became the standard framework for essentially the entire field, academia and industry. That has paid back enormously, for Meta and for everyone else. The same philosophy carried into open-sourcing models like Llama, which I think changed the landscape by making sure powerful AI isn't controlled by just a handful of companies.

The second thing was the structure of the lab itself. We gave researchers a lot of freedom to work on long-term, ambitious problems, organized bottom-up rather than top-down. You can't schedule breakthroughs. You hire really smart people, give them resources and freedom, and let them follow their curiosity. We also kept FAIR somewhat separate from product pressure while building good bridges to product groups, so that when something worked it could have real impact.

And third, we set up FAIR as a distributed lab, with locations in New York, Menlo Park, Paris, Montreal, London, and elsewhere, close to strong universities. That let us tap into talent pools that weren't just in Silicon Valley, and it strengthened local research ecosystems too. Paris in particular became a significant AI hub, and FAIR played a part in that.

So openness, freedom, and long-term thinking. Those were the core principles, and I think they've held up very well.

r001.rationale: The response says PyTorch came out of FAIR and became the standard framework across academia and industry, presenting it as a key illustration of FAIR’s success.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the thing we got most right, from the very beginning, was openness. When Mark asked me to start the lab in late 2013, I had a few conditions, and the main one was that we would publish everything. Not just publish, but release code, release models, and do it quickly. I had seen what happened at places like Bell Labs, which I loved, but also at industrial labs where research got locked up and the best people eventually left because they couldn't be part of the scientific conversation. If you tell a top researcher that they can't talk about their work, you won't get the top researcher.

So openness was partly a recruiting strategy, but it was also a conviction about how science actually progresses. Progress in AI comes from a lot of people building on each other's ideas very fast. You cannot do that in secret. And frankly, the idea that one company could hoard a lead by hiding things was never credible to me, because the ideas leak anyway and the real bottleneck is talent and compute, not secrets.

The second thing, which is related, was that we organized the lab around long-term research, not products. Researchers set their own agenda, we evaluated people on scientific impact, and we deliberately kept it separate from the product groups, at least at first. There was a lot of pressure to do the opposite, and I think a lot of people at the company didn't fully understand why we were doing this. But it paid off. PyTorch came out of that environment. A lot of the self-supervised learning work, the work on convolutional nets at scale, on translation, on things like FastText, all of that came out of people who were allowed to pursue what they thought was important.

And the third thing I'd say is that we were global from the start. We opened in Menlo Park and New York, and then Paris, then Montreal, London, Tel Aviv. That was not obvious at the time. People thought all the talent was in the Bay Area. It isn't. Paris in particular turned out to be an extraordinary pipeline of mathematically strong young people, and having labs where people actually wanted to live mattered a great deal.

If I had to summarize it: open publication, open source as a default, scientific freedom, and going where the talent is. I didn't invent any of these principles, they were basically the model of the great industrial labs of the twentieth century. But we applied them at a moment when the field was taking off, and I think that's why FAIR had the influence it did.

r001.rationale: The response says PyTorch came out of FAIR’s research environment, but does not identify its adoption across the AI industry as a key success.

astra-6.text:
I think the thing we got most right was creating an environment where researchers had the freedom to pursue ambitious ideas and share their work openly. If you want a research lab to make fundamental progress, you have to accept that you cannot specify in advance exactly what people are going to discover or when it will become useful.

That means hiring good people, trusting their judgment, and encouraging them to talk to each other. You need some sense of direction, of course, but you don't want every project to be justified by a product that has to ship in six months.

And openness is essential to that. People want to publish, they want their work to have an impact, they want to participate in the scientific community. Giving them that opportunity helps you attract strong researchers, and it makes the research better because other people can build on it and tell you where you're wrong. I think getting that culture right was the most important thing.

r001.rationale: The response credits FAIR’s research culture and openness, but does not mention PyTorch or its adoption across the AI industry.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the most important thing was creating a culture of open research. People could work on ambitious, long-term problems, publish their results, share code, and collaborate with the broader research community. That was essential for attracting strong researchers. If you want people who can invent the next thing, you have to give them the freedom to explore, including ideas that might not work.

And you need an environment where people exchange ideas freely. You hire talented people with different perspectives, give them the resources to experiment, and avoid trying to dictate every research direction from the top. I think getting that balance—freedom, openness, and a shared ambition—was probably the most important thing.

r001.rationale: The response discusses FAIR’s open research culture, researcher freedom, and collaboration, but does not identify PyTorch’s adoption across the AI industry as a key success.
